# Choosing and forming the vehicle {#sec-blp-vehicles}

> *Assessment objective 1: starting a new business through the vehicle of a company, partnership,
> LLP or as a sole trader.*

## Why the choice matters

A client starting a business is really choosing among four trade-offs, and almost every exam
question on this topic is testing one of them.

**Liability.** Will the founders' personal assets be exposed if the business fails? This is the
first question most clients ask and the one they most often misunderstand.

**Tax.** Is the business itself taxed, or are the owners taxed on its profits directly? The
difference between a *transparent* vehicle and an *opaque* one drives a great deal of real-world
structuring advice.

**Formality and cost.** Some vehicles come into existence by accident. Others require registration,
filings, accounts and a constitution.

**Publicity and control.** Incorporation buys limited liability at the price of putting your
accounts, officers and ownership on a public register.

## The four vehicles at a glance

|  | Sole trader | General partnership | LLP | Private company |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Separate legal personality | No | No | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Owners' liability | Unlimited, personal | Unlimited; joint (debts), joint and several (wrongs) | Limited | Limited to amount unpaid on shares |
| How it comes into being | Simply trading | **By conduct** — no formality needed | Incorporation at Companies House | Incorporation at Companies House |
| Governing statute | — | Partnership Act 1890 | Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 | Companies Act 2006 |
| Taxed as | Income tax on profits | Transparent — partners taxed individually | **Transparent** — members taxed individually | Corporation tax; shareholders taxed on distributions |
| Public filing | None | None | Accounts, confirmation statement | Accounts, confirmation statement |
| Constitution | — | Partnership agreement, or PA 1890 defaults | Members' agreement, or default regulations | Articles of association |

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
The LLP is the hybrid, and the hybrid is where questions live. It **is** a body corporate with
separate legal personality and limited liability — but it is **taxed transparently**, like a
partnership. Any option telling you an LLP pays corporation tax on its profits is wrong. Any option
telling you an LLP has no separate legal personality is also wrong. Candidates who have half-learned
the point reliably pick one or the other.
:::

## The sole trader

There is nothing to form. A person who starts trading on their own account is a sole trader, and
the business has no legal existence separate from them. Its assets are their assets, its debts are
their debts, and its profits are their income, charged to income tax with Class 2 and Class 4
National Insurance contributions.

The absence of separate personality is the whole point. A sole trader cannot contract with their own
business, cannot be employed by it, and cannot limit their exposure to its creditors. Against that,
there is no registration, no constitution, no public filing and no audit.

Trading names are regulated even here: the restrictions on business names in Part 41 of the
Companies Act 2006 apply to sole traders and partnerships, not only to companies.

## The general partnership

### How it arises

Section 1(1) of the Partnership Act 1890 defines partnership as *"the relation which subsists
between persons carrying on a business in common with a view of profit"*.

Read that carefully. It says nothing about agreement, documentation, or intention to form a
partnership. If the elements are present, the relation exists.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Partnership arises **by conduct**. A scenario in which two people never signed anything, never used
the word "partnership", and would deny being partners can still be a partnership — and each will
then be liable for the other's business debts without limit. The examiner's favourite version is
two friends who "just started working together". Look for business, in common, with a view of
profit. Sharing gross returns alone does not create a partnership (s.2(2)); receipt of a share of
profits is *prima facie* evidence but not conclusive (s.2(3)).
:::

In England and Wales a partnership has **no separate legal personality**. The firm is the partners.
(Scots law differs — a distraction the examiner sometimes uses.)

### The default terms

Where the partners have no agreement, or their agreement is silent, the Act supplies terms. These
are heavily examined because the question usually turns on what happens *absent* an agreement.

| Section | Default rule |
|---|---|
| s.24(1) | Partners share **equally** in capital and profits, and contribute equally to losses — regardless of unequal capital contributions |
| s.24(5) | Every partner may take part in management |
| s.24(6) | **No** partner is entitled to a salary |
| s.24(7) | **No** new partner may be introduced without **unanimous** consent |
| s.24(8) | Ordinary matters decided by **majority**; a change in the **nature of the business** requires **unanimity** |
| s.25 | **No** majority may expel a partner unless the agreement says so |
| s.26 | A partnership at will may be dissolved by **any** partner giving notice — immediately |
| s.28 | Duty to render true accounts and full information |
| s.29 | Duty to account for private profits from the partnership |
| s.30 | Duty not to compete with the firm |

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Section 24(1) is the one that produces the unfair-looking answer. A partner who contributed £90,000
of the capital and a partner who contributed £10,000 share profits **equally** unless they agreed
otherwise. Candidates instinctively apportion by contribution. The Act does not.
:::

### Authority and liability to outsiders

Section 5 is the partnership equivalent of agency. A partner's act binds the firm where it is *for
carrying on in the usual way business of the kind carried on by the firm* — **unless** the partner
had no authority **and** the third party either knew that or did not know or believe them to be a
partner. Both limbs are needed to escape liability.

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example"}
Anna, Ben and Chi are partners in a firm of architects. Their agreement says no partner may commit
the firm to more than £5,000 without the others' consent. Anna orders £12,000 of drafting software
from a supplier who knows nothing of the restriction.

Is the firm bound? Ordering professional software is an act for carrying on in the usual way the
business of a firm of architects, so s.5 is engaged. Anna lacked actual authority — but the supplier
neither knew that nor doubted she was a partner. **The firm is bound.** The internal restriction is
enforceable between the partners, not against the supplier. Anna is liable to indemnify her partners.

Change one fact: the supplier had been told of the £5,000 limit. Now both limbs are satisfied and
the firm is not bound.
:::

Related provisions worth knowing precisely:

- **s.9** — partners are jointly liable for the firm's **debts and obligations**.
- **ss.10–12** — partners are jointly and severally liable for **wrongs** committed in the ordinary
  course of business.
- **s.14** — a person who represents themselves, or knowingly allows themselves to be represented,
  as a partner is liable as one to anyone who gives credit on the faith of it (*holding out*).
- **s.17(1)** — an **incoming** partner is **not** liable for debts incurred before they joined.
- **s.17(2)** — an **outgoing** partner remains liable for debts incurred while they were a partner.
- **s.36** — and remains liable for **later** debts to those who dealt with the firm before, unless
  notice is given: actual notice to existing customers, and *London Gazette* notice for the world.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
The retiring partner who "told everyone" is a standing favourite. Retirement alone does not end
exposure to future creditors who previously dealt with the firm. Actual notice to them plus Gazette
notice is what does it.
:::

## The limited liability partnership

The LLP was created by the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 for professional firms that
wanted limited liability without becoming companies. It is genuinely a hybrid.

- It is a **body corporate** with separate legal personality and unlimited capacity (s.1 LLPA 2000).
- Its owners are **members**, not partners. At least two are **designated members**, carrying the
  administrative duties a company secretary would otherwise bear.
- It is formed by **incorporation** — two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful
  business with a view of profit, subscribing to an incorporation document delivered to the
  Registrar.
- Its internal affairs are governed by a members' agreement; where there is none, default
  regulations supply terms broadly mirroring the PA 1890 defaults.
- It files accounts and a confirmation statement, so it trades **publicity** for **limited
  liability** in the same bargain a company makes.
- It is **tax transparent**: the LLP itself pays no corporation tax, and members are taxed
  individually on their shares of profit.

The limited liability is not absolute. Section 214A of the Insolvency Act 1986 allows a liquidator
to claw back withdrawals made by a member in the two years before winding up, where the member knew
or had reasonable ground to believe the LLP was, or would become, unable to pay its debts.

## Companies

### Private and public

A private company limited by shares is the default vehicle for a small business. An unlisted public
company is rarer and mostly examined by contrast.

| | Private limited | Public |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum share capital | None | £50,000, at least 25% paid up |
| May trade from incorporation | Yes | No — needs a trading certificate under s.761 CA 2006 |
| Company secretary | Optional | **Required** |
| Written resolutions | Available | **Not** available |
| AGM | Not required | **Required** |
| Offer shares to the public | **Prohibited** | Permitted |

### Separate legal personality

*Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd* [1897] AC 22 is the foundation. A properly incorporated company is a
legal person distinct from its shareholders, even where one person owns and controls it entirely.
Mr Salomon's company owed money to Mr Salomon, and he ranked as a secured creditor ahead of the
unsecured ones. The House of Lords held the company was validly formed and the consequences followed.

Two consequences are examined more often than the principle itself:

- *Macaura v Northern Assurance Co Ltd* [1925] AC 619 — a shareholder has **no insurable interest**
  in the company's assets. Macaura insured timber in his own name; the company owned it; his claim
  failed.
- *Lee v Lee's Air Farming Ltd* [1961] AC 12 — a person can be simultaneously the controlling
  shareholder, sole director, **and an employee** of their own company. Lee's widow recovered as the
  dependant of a worker killed in the course of employment.

### Piercing the corporate veil

The courts will disregard separate personality only in very narrow circumstances. *Prest v Petrodel
Resources Ltd* [2013] UKSC 34 restated the law and drew a distinction that is the whole of the
modern doctrine:

- The **concealment** principle: the court looks *behind* the company to identify who is really
  acting. This is not piercing at all — it is ordinary fact-finding, and it is always available.
- The **evasion** principle: the court disregards the company where a person **under an existing
  legal obligation** deliberately interposes a company to **frustrate or evade** it. This is the
  only true piercing, and it is exceptional.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
"The company was a one-man company", "the company was a sham", "the shareholder controlled
everything", "it would be just and equitable" — none of these is sufficient. Look for a
**pre-existing obligation** that the company was interposed to escape. Absent that, the veil stands,
however unattractive the outcome.
:::

Statute achieves by other means much of what the common law refuses: wrongful trading (s.214
Insolvency Act 1986) and fraudulent trading (s.213) impose personal liability on directors without
disturbing the company's separate personality. Those are covered in @sec-blp-termination.

### Formation

A company is formed under s.7 CA 2006 by one or more persons subscribing to a memorandum of
association and complying with the registration requirements. What is delivered to the Registrar:

1. **Memorandum of association** (s.8) — now a short prescribed-form document in which the
   subscribers state that they wish to form a company and agree to become members, taking at least
   one share each. It is a **historical record** of formation; it is *not* the company's
   constitution and cannot be amended.
2. **Application for registration** (s.9) — form IN01, stating the proposed name, whether liability
   is limited, whether the company is private or public, the situation of the registered office
   (England and Wales, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland), a statement of capital and initial
   shareholdings, a statement of proposed officers, and a statement of the intended registered
   office address.
3. **Articles of association**, unless the relevant Model Articles are adopted in full by default.
4. **Statement of compliance** (s.13).
5. The registration fee.

The Registrar issues a **certificate of incorporation** (s.15), which is **conclusive evidence**
that the registration requirements were met (s.15(4)). The company exists from the date on the
certificate (s.16).

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
The memorandum under the 2006 Act is not the constitutional document it was under the 1985 Act. The
company's constitution is its **articles**. An option describing the memorandum as containing the
objects clause, or as amendable by special resolution, is testing whether you know the regime
changed.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Verify before relying on this"}
The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 introduced identity verification for
directors, persons with significant control and those filing at Companies House, together with
enhanced Registrar powers. These provisions have been commencing in **stages**. Check what is in
force, and — see @sec-cutoff — whether it falls before your sitting's examinable law cut-off, before
treating any of it as the answer.
:::

### The articles

The articles are the company's constitution. If none are registered, or the registered articles do
not exclude or modify them, the relevant **Model Articles** apply by default (s.20 CA 2006).

**Section 33** gives the articles contractual force: the provisions of a company's constitution bind
the company and its members as if there were covenants by each to observe them. The contract is
enforceable only in respect of **membership rights** — a member suing in some other capacity, such
as as a solicitor engaged by the company, cannot rely on s.33.

**Amendment** requires a **special resolution** (s.21) — 75%. Three limits:

- A member cannot be bound by an alteration made after they became a member which requires them to
  take more shares or increases their liability, unless they agree in writing (s.25).
- Provisions may be **entrenched** (s.22), requiring a more restrictive procedure than a special
  resolution. Entrenchment can be introduced only on formation or by **unanimous** agreement.
- The power must be exercised *bona fide* for the benefit of the company as a whole (*Allen v Gold
  Reefs of West Africa Ltd* [1900] 1 Ch 656).

A copy of any amended articles must be filed within 15 days.

### The company name

Sections 53–57 CA 2006 restrict names: a private limited company's name must end with "limited" or
"ltd" (or the Welsh equivalents *cyfyngedig* / *cyf*); a name that is the same as one already
registered is prohibited; and certain sensitive or offensive words require approval. A company may
change its name by **special resolution** (s.77), and the change takes effect when the Registrar
issues a new certificate of incorporation on the change of name.

### Off-the-shelf or tailor-made

A shelf company is bought ready-formed and then adapted: the subscriber shares are transferred, new
directors appointed, the old ones resign, the name is changed and the articles amended. Formation
from scratch avoids that unwinding but takes slightly longer. Electronic incorporation has narrowed
the gap so far that the shelf company is now mostly of historical interest — but it appears in
questions, and the point being tested is usually the *sequence* of steps needed to adapt one.

## The solicitor's position

Two conduct issues recur in formation scenarios, and both are worth more marks than their length
suggests.

**Who is the client?** Once a company is incorporated it is a client distinct from its founders. A
solicitor instructed to "set up the business for Anna and Ben" must be clear whether they act for
Anna, for Ben, for both, or for the company — and the answer changes who they owe duties to when the
founders fall out.

**Conflict of interest.** Acting for two or more founders whose interests may diverge — on
shareholdings, on control, on what happens if one leaves — engages the conflict provisions of the
Code of Conduct. The safe course, and usually the right answer, is to advise each to take independent
advice on the terms of the shareholders' agreement, rather than to proceed on the basis that
everyone is currently friendly.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
The client's consent does not cure everything. Where there is a conflict, or a significant risk of
one, the exceptions permitting a solicitor to act are narrow and depend on the clients having a
substantially common interest or competing for the same objective, plus informed consent and
appropriate safeguards. An option that says "may act because both clients consented in writing" is
usually incomplete.
:::

## Test yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Five questions — answers hidden until you open them"}

**1.** Priya contributed £80,000 to a partnership; Sam contributed £20,000. There is no written
agreement. The firm makes £50,000 profit. How is it shared?

**2.** A retiring partner writes to all the firm's existing customers announcing her retirement but
places no notice in the *London Gazette*. A new customer, who had never dealt with the firm before,
later contracts with it and is unpaid. Is the retired partner liable?

**3.** A father, subject to a court order requiring him to transfer a specific property to his
daughter, transfers it instead to a company he wholly owns. Will the court pierce the veil?

**4.** An LLP makes £400,000 of profit. Which tax is charged on that profit, and on whom?

**5.** A company's articles contain a provision requiring 90% approval to remove a director. The
provision was inserted after incorporation by special resolution passed on a 78% vote, with no
entrenchment procedure followed. Is it effective as an entrenched provision?

---

**Answers**

**1.** Equally — £25,000 each. Section 24(1) provides for equal sharing of profits regardless of
unequal capital contributions, and there is no agreement displacing it. The instinct to apportion
80:20 is the trap.

**2.** No. Section 36 protects those who **dealt with the firm before** the retirement, and requires
actual notice to them; the *Gazette* notice protects against **new** customers. A customer who never
dealt with the firm before the retirement cannot have relied on her membership, so the absence of
Gazette notice does not make her liable here. (Note the contrast: had it been an *existing* customer
who received no notice, she would be exposed.)

**3.** Yes, on the evasion principle in *Prest v Petrodel*. There is a **pre-existing legal
obligation** — the court order — and the company was interposed to frustrate it. This is the narrow
case in which the veil is genuinely pierced.

**4.** None on the LLP itself. An LLP is **tax transparent**: each member is charged to income tax
on their share of the profit, whether or not it is drawn. Corporation tax is not in point.

**5.** No. Entrenchment under s.22 may be introduced only on formation or by **unanimous** agreement
of all the members. A 78% special resolution is enough to *amend* the articles but not to *entrench*
a provision, so the 90% requirement is not protected against later removal by ordinary special
resolution.

:::
